fact: LeBron James averages 26.8 points and 7.5 rebounds a game for his career — high scoring with real but not elite rebounding. Wilt Chamberlain (30.1 / 22.9) is the only player in NBA history to average 30+ points and 20+ rebounds for a full career. Dennis Rodman (7.3 / 13.1) is the mirror image — elite rebounding, modest scoring.

LeBron James averages 7.4 assists a game to go with his scoring — genuinely rare playmaking for a top-5 all-time scorer. Chris Paul (16.8 / 9.2) built his whole career around exactly that combination at a smaller scale. Rodman (7.3 / 1.8) shows the opposite: a non-playmaking specialist.

LeBron James sits almost exactly in the middle on both assists (7.4) and rebounds (7.5) — a genuine do-everything profile rather than a specialist in either direction. Chris Paul (9.2 / 4.4) leans hard toward playmaking, Rodman (1.8 / 13.1) leans hard toward rebounding, and almost no one in NBA history is this balanced across both at LeBron's scoring volume.

Jonathan Taylor's 2021 season is the counterintuitive one here: his 106.5 rushing yards per game is actually the lowest of these four seasons, yet his 18 rushing touchdowns is the highest — the 17-game season gave him an extra game, and a huge share of his team's goal-line work. Adrian Peterson's 2012 MVP season (131.1 YPG) is the opposite profile: gaining more yards per game than anyone here, but with the fewest touchdowns.
source: Pro Football Reference / StatMuse season totals. Yards-per-game computed from confirmed season yardage ÷ games played.

fact: Scottie Pippen's 2.0 steals and 0.8 blocks a game is a genuinely rare wing profile — enough blocks to suggest a rim-protecting big, delivered by a 6'8" forward who also picked pockets like a guard. Dikembe Mutombo (0.4 / 2.8) and John Stockton (2.2 / 0.2) are the two specialist extremes this pairing usually produces: a pure rim-protector and a pure ball-hawk. Hakeem Olajuwon (1.7 / 3.1) is the rare exception who tops both — a center with a guard's hands and a shot-blocker's timing.

xLabel: Career field goal attempts per game
fact: Michael Jordan took more shots per game (22.9) than anyone else here — even more than Allen Iverson (21.8), the standard reference for a pure volume scorer. But his efficiency (56.9 TS%) sits well below the elite tier: Stephen Curry (62.6) gets nearly as many shots up at a far higher efficiency, and DeAndre Jordan (64.4) shows the opposite extreme — a role player who barely shoots (5.1 attempts a game) but converts at an absurd rate, mostly dunks and putbacks. Jordan's greatness came from volume and shot difficulty, not from posting efficiency numbers like the specialists at either end of this chart.
source: StatMuse career true shooting percentage and field goal attempts per game (regular season).

fact: Jameis Winston throws touchdowns at almost the same rate as Brett Favre (4.8% vs. 5.0%) — but his interception rate (3.5%) is even higher than Favre's, the quarterback whose whole reputation is built on high-risk gunslinging. Alex Smith (2.1% / 3.8%) is the pure game-manager opposite: low risk, low reward. Aaron Rodgers (1.4% / 6.0%) shows the tradeoff isn't actually mandatory — the best touchdown rate in this set paired with the best career interception percentage in NFL history.
source: StatMuse career passing touchdown percentage and interception percentage.

fact: Barry Bonds holds the all-time home run record (762) — more than even Babe Ruth's 714 — but his .298 career batting average trails Ruth's .342 by a wide margin, and Dave Kingman's raw power (442 HR on a .236 average) shows that home run totals alone don't tell the whole story. Tony Gwynn (.338 / 135) is the pure-contact opposite: one of the best pure hitters ever, with a fraction of the power. Ruth remains the rare player who tops the field on both axes at once.
source: StatMuse career batting average and home run totals.

fact: Zach Randolph made just 2 All-Star teams in his career — yet his 16.6 career points per game is basically identical to Joe Johnson's 16.0 (7 All-Star nods) and Vince Carter's 16.7 (8 nods). All-Star selections reward more than raw scoring average — team success, era, and position all factor in — and Randolph's Memphis grit-and-grind identity earned him far less recognition than his actual production. Karl Malone (14 AS, 25.0 PPG) anchors the other extreme: a player whose selections actually matched his all-time-great scoring.
source: StatMuse career per-game averages and career All-Star selection counts.

fact: Anquan Boldin made only 3 Pro Bowls in his career, but his 13,779 receiving yards is within shouting distance of Randy Moss's 15,292 — a player who made twice as many Pro Bowls. Boldin's game was built on contested catches and physicality rather than the highlight-reel speed that tends to win Pro Bowl votes, and it cost him recognition his production arguably earned. Jerry Rice (13 PB, 22,895 yards) remains the standard nobody else in NFL history has matched.
source: StatMuse / Pro Football Reference career Pro Bowl selections and receiving yards.

fact: Bobby Abreu and Adam Dunn each made exactly 2 All-Star teams — but Dunn hit 174 more career home runs (462 to Abreu's 288). Abreu's value came from on-base percentage, doubles, and stolen bases rather than pure power, a game sabermetricians rate highly but All-Star voters historically haven't rewarded the same way as a big home run total. Griffey (13 AS, 630 HR) and Rodriguez (14 AS, 696 HR) show what it looks like when a player's power and his recognition actually line up.
source: StatMuse career All-Star selections and home run totals.
